html:
An open-air observatory of nineteen large masonry instruments in Jaipur, India, built by the Rajput ruler Jai Singh II and finished in 1734.

The instruments are buildings: stone and marble walls, quadrants, bowls and arcs, sized so that the naked eye can read the sky precisely. They measure time, track the sun, find the positions of stars and planets, and predict eclipses. The largest, the Samrat Yantra, is a giant sundial about 27 metres high whose shadow moves visibly across its scale.

Jai Singh built five such observatories, at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura; Jaipur's is the biggest and best kept. He studied Islamic astronomy, including the tables of Ulugh Beg made at Samarkand, and Sanskrit works, and had European books brought to him. He used his results to correct the calendar and the astronomical tables for the Mughal emperor. By then European astronomers were using telescopes, so the observatory was the last great work of a naked-eye tradition. It is a World Heritage Site.
sum: An open-air observatory of nineteen large masonry instruments in Jaipur, India, built by the Rajput ruler Jai Singh II and finished in 1734.
